summary: Seven conditions an operator would recognise, each declared with the objectives it is expected to move and the objectives expected to stay flat. The flat list is the half that makes a signature falsifiable: three of these conditions move nothing this estate has an objective for, and each of those says why rather than being left out. Injecting one is the fixture's job and changing the estate to make one injectable is refused - where that refusal costs a condition, the mechanism records it.

scenarios.title: The ledger answers correctly and far too slowly
scenarios.mechanism: A TCP proxy in the fixture sits between the gateway and the ledger and holds every response for the declared delay before forwarding it. Nothing in the estate is reconfigured beyond the address the gateway is given, which is already an environment variable it reads at boot.
scenarios.rationale: The misleading graph here is the ledger's own. `ledger_posting_latency_seconds` times what the ledger did, and the ledger did it just as fast as ever - the delay is in front of it. An operator reading the ledger's dashboard during this condition sees a component in perfect health while every customer waits a second and a half, and the only place the truth appears is the edge. That is the whole argument for measuring latency where the customer is, which is also why the workload driver stamps it from the intended send time.

scenarios.title: The ledger is gone and its own success rate looks perfect
scenarios.mechanism: The fixture sends SIGSTOP to the ledger's process group for the declared window and SIGCONT afterwards. The group rather than the process, because gradlew execs a JVM and signalling the wrapper leaves the JVM running. The gateway, the database and the broker keep running, so the estate is partially rather than wholly down and the driver keeps offering the day it planned. A suspended process is not an unreachable one - it holds its listening socket and the kernel keeps accepting - and what that costs the signature is the point of running it.
scenarios.rationale: A ratio computed from a component's own counters cannot fall while the component is not counting. `ledger_transfers_total` stops advancing entirely, so the ledger's success rate over the window is whatever it was before the outage started - which reads as a healthy ledger rather than an absent one. This is the single most important thing to have seen before reading a dashboard under pressure, and the reason a component's availability has to be judged from outside it. **Revised by WP-24c with the measurement in hand.** The first sweep declared that judging from outside would move `SLO-GATEWAY-AVAILABILITY`, and it did not: availability stayed at 1.00000 over 34 322 requests while `SLO-GATEWAY-LATENCY` went from met to missed at 0.95283, 4.72x its budget. A suspended process is not a refused connection. It holds its listening socket, the kernel keeps accepting, and every request that arrives during the window is answered late rather than not at all - so the outage arrives at the edge as latency and never as failure. Judging from outside is still the right instruction; the graph it moves is the other one.

scenarios.title: Money moves, events stop, and only one graph notices
scenarios.mechanism: The fixture pauses the broker container for the declared window. The relay's send times out, the batch stops at the first failure to preserve per-key order, and the rows stay undispatched - which is the real production shape of this failure rather than a simulation of it.
scenarios.rationale: The outbox exists so that the domain event is written in the same transaction as the postings, which means a broker outage costs the estate nothing at the moment it happens - every transfer still commits, and every customer-facing objective holds. The cost is entirely downstream and entirely invisible until somebody looks at the age of the oldest unpublished row. `ledger-observability.md` claims the lag rather than the count is the one to page on; this is the condition that either demonstrates that or corrects it.

scenarios.title: The scorer stops consuming and its completeness stays at one
scenarios.mechanism: The fixture suspends the scorer process for the declared window with SIGSTOP and resumes it afterwards. The broker keeps accepting, the ledger keeps relaying, and the consumer group's committed offset stops advancing - a real lag rather than a stopped producer.
scenarios.movesNothingBecause: The scorer publishes no consumer-lag metric, and `SLO-FRAUD-DECISION-COMPLETENESS` is decisions over decisions plus malformed - a ratio of what was consumed, not of what was offered. Consuming nothing leaves it exactly where it was. Nothing in the catalogue is stated over the gap between what the ledger published and what the scorer read, so this condition is invisible to every objective the estate declares.
scenarios.rationale: A completeness ratio over consumed events is the classic denominator mistake: it answers `of the work I did, how much did I finish` when the question is `did I do the work`. The objective is not wrong - it catches a malformed producer, which is what it was written for - it simply cannot see a consumer that has stopped. Recording that here is worth more than adding a metric, because the gap is the finding and closing it silently would hide what the exercise was for.

scenarios.title: The edge refuses thousands of customers at full availability
scenarios.mechanism: The fixture offers the declared rate through the gateway across the declared number of token subjects, alongside the day the driver is already executing. The limiter is per subject and route class per ADR 0006, so a single subject exhausts one bucket and the storm is a customer; spread across many it is an outage.
scenarios.movesNothingBecause: A 429 is deliberately on the good side of `SLO-GATEWAY-AVAILABILITY` - its own rationale says so, because retrying into a limiter converts a working control into a stampede. Refusals are counted by `tessera_gateway_refusals_total`, which the catalogue carries as a signal with no objective. So a storm that turns customers away at any volume moves nothing the estate has promised anything about.
scenarios.rationale: This is the flattest of the seven and the most useful to have seen. Every objective holds, the error budget is untouched, and a proportion of customers cannot use the bank. The decision to count a refusal as success is right and is argued in the objective's own rationale; what it costs is that availability alone cannot distinguish a working estate from a throttled one, and only the refusal signal beside it can.

scenarios.title: Every transfer queues for a connection that is not free
scenarios.mechanism: The injector opens a session on the database container and holds the declared lock on the declared table for the window, then rolls back. Writers block inside the ledger while holding a pooled connection, so the pool drains from the inside rather than from a changed pool size - the ledger's Hikari configuration is not touched.
scenarios.rationale: `SLO-LEDGER-POOL-HEADROOM` is stated as the earliest of the ledger's four objectives to break, and this condition is the test of that ordering. SHARE rather than ACCESS EXCLUSIVE is deliberate: readers keep passing, so the signature is a queue rather than an outage. **Revised by WP-24c with the measurement in hand**, and it is what F-83 saw in one run and a second sweep confirmed: the condition is invisible in both of the ledger's own signals and plain at the edge. `SLO-LEDGER-POSTING-LATENCY` degraded to 0.99398 against 0.99 - real, 0.60x of its budget, inside the line - so it is declared flat. `SLO-GATEWAY-LATENCY` missed at 0.94141, 5.86x its budget, because a blocked writer holds its pooled connection and everything behind it queues for one, reads included, and reads are three quarters of the day. `SLO-LEDGER-POOL-HEADROOM` stays declared: it is what the condition is named for, and a gauge bracketed by two scrapes reads 0 at both ends whatever happened between them. That is `inconclusive` rather than contradicted, and closing it is F-82.

scenarios.title: The two sides of the cut-off disagree about which day it is
scenarios.mechanism: This fixture cannot produce this condition and the injector says so rather than pretending. PostgreSQL stamps the value date from its own `now()`, so moving the two sides of the boundary apart means moving a clock inside a container - which needs SYS_TIME on a kernel shared with the host, or a faketime shim in the image. Both change the estate rather than the fixture, and WP-24's Constraint refuses them. Skewing the driver's own date is not the same condition: the ledger stamps its value dates itself.
scenarios.movesNothingBecause: The two objectives a boundary disagreement would break belong to `recon` and `reporting`, and both are batch jobs that do not run inside a compressed nine-hour window - F-77's remaining half. Their metrics go to a node_exporter textfile rather than to anything a run scrapes, so a report over this run answers `nothing happened` for both no matter what the skew did.
scenarios.rationale: ADR 0015 defines the cut-off as the set of transfer references in the movement file rather than as a time of day, precisely so that a clock disagreement cannot silently move the boundary. This condition exercises the claim from the other side: a skew that would break a timestamp-based cut-off should leave a reference-based one intact. That it cannot be observed inside a compressed window is the second finding, and the one that says what closing the rest of F-77 is worth.
